message.reasoning:
I'm reconstructing the layout of this old Brazilian newspaper page, aiming to replicate its header and three-column structure while transcribing the visible text as closely as possible into the appropriate sections.

I'm noting the request for a distinction medal for the soldier who jumped into the sea at Santos to save a drowning fireman, plus the transmission of documents about yellow fever cases in Araraquara and orders regarding police reinforcements there and in Santos.

I'm also seeing references to municipal correspondence from Remédios da Ponte do Tietê and Santo Antônio da Cachoeira, followed by a new section where the Secretary of Justice sets forage distribution tables for the Public Force and Police animals starting April 5th.

I'm noting there's an observation that pastured animals lose their ration of alfafa, canna, milho and sal, followed by the official signature and date from the Secretaria da Justiça. There's also a note about forwarding the provisional table to the police chief and Almoxarifado, plus a separate act raising the daily food allowance for poor prisoners at the Agudos jail from 800 réis to 1$300, effective April 1st.

Now I'm reading a communication from the Secretaria dos Negócios da Justiça to the Brigada Policial commander, dated March 31, 1900, announcing that the new state stamp tax regulation (decree n. 759) takes effect April 2nd, requiring petitions to bear stamps of 1$000 for the first page and 200 réis for subsequent pages.

I continue reviewing similar circulars sent to the police chief and interior corps commander, followed by a list of payments requested from the Secretary of Finance, including a monthly 30$000 payment to José Antonio da Costa since January 1st for renting a building used as barracks and jail in Platina.

Now I'm going through more rental payments: 35$000 to Jorge Alleu Jeffery for a barracks/jail building in Bello Monte, 60$000 to Manoel Joaquim Gonçalves for the Nodoa police post, and 60$000 to d. Anna Maria Caldeira for the Morro Pellado barracks covering January and February.

I'm also cataloging refunds owed to former soldiers for uniform discounts and back pay, listing names like Caetano Pestrini, José Joaquim de Lemos, Francisco Martins de Oliveira, Gregorio Vasques, Adolf Pereira, and Raymundo Antonio de Souza with their respective amounts, continuing into a third column with José Antonio Sampaio and José Pedro de Campos.

Now I'm looking at officios forwarded from police delegates in Rio Claro, Atibaia, and Nuporanga regarding payment of food allowances for poor prisoners, followed by requerimentos from Diogo Antonio de Arruda Mendes seeking payment for medicines supplied to prisoners in Dous Corregos, and from J. G. dos Santos Figueiredo for supplies to the Mocóca jail.

Continuing through the requerimentos, there's Francisco Ferreira da Silva, a soldier of the interior police corps, requesting back pay of 104$680, and Francisco de Salles Gomes seeking 260$000 for medical services to poor prisoners in Tatuhy. Then declarations follow about contracting Mari Garrido to supply food to prisoners in Annapolis at a thousand réis daily, and a note to the police chief explaining that a request from the Jundiahy delegate couldn't be attended due to lack of funds.

Now I'm looking at more administrative responses: about a bell needed for the Jundiahy jail, instructions for the owner of a building serving as barracks and jail in Taquary to formally request payment for 1898 rent, and authorization to the Superintendência de Obras Públicas to spend 5:050$123 on repairs to the São João da Boa Vista jail. There's also authorization for the Força Pública's warehouse chief to supply various office items to the Penitenciária.

I'm moving into the March 31, 1900 expediente, which includes the Secretary of Agriculture requesting payment for supplies furnished to the Repartição de Águas e Exgotos in February, listing amounts owed to specific companies like the Companhia Mechanica e Importadora de S. Paulo and Espindola, Siqueira & Comp.
